rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all 10 compounds and identify limiting peak pairs without excessive retention. The observed elution window will guide gradient trimming and subsequent slope and temperature tests.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the two limiting pairs respond to a shallower slope. The current last peak at 7.16 minutes leaves room to improve resolution while aiming to keep all peaks within 10 minutes.

The limiting pair improves strongly with a shallower gradient, so reduce the slope further. Raising the starting organic fraction trims low-organic time and should help keep the last peak below 10 minutes while retaining adequate early-peak separation.

Injection 3 reached the maximum CRF; now test a shorter fully resolved method by raising the starting organic fraction while preserving gradient slope and temperature. This should advance the late peak, though early-pair and critical-pair resolution must be checked.

Make the gradient shallower to restore critical-pair resolution at the higher starting organic fraction. The last peak at 8.59 minutes provides room to extend the gradient while targeting full resolution before 10 minutes.

Hold the gradient fixed and test whether a modest temperature increase shortens retention while preserving full resolution. This isolates temperature selectivity for the marginally resolved pair, with two maximum-score methods already established.

Test whether a larger temperature shift restores critical-pair separation after an elution-order reversal and shortens the fully resolved method. Use injection 3’s lower starting organic fraction to protect early-peak retention at the higher temperature.

Reduce temperature to separate the new limiting pair seen at 60 C while aiming to preserve separation of the previously limiting cluster. This intermediate temperature could deliver full resolution with a last peak earlier than either established maximum-score method.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the pair at R = 1.41, with enough retention-time headroom to target elution before 10 minutes. Check that the nearby pair currently at R = 1.74 remains fully resolved as selectivity shifts.
Use a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9 to seek full resolution with an earlier last peak. The limiting resolutions should remain above 1.5 while the last peak should elute around 9 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 10’s gradient slope to seek earlier elution at the maximum CRF. Check early-peak separation and both close middle pairs, since changing the starting fraction can alter their resolution.

Test a lower starting organic fraction at 60 C to improve the middle pair that was nearly co-eluting in injection 7. The strong starting-fraction effect observed at 55 C suggests this may restore full resolution while retaining the high-temperature time advantage.

Combine a lower starting organic fraction with a shorter gradient at 55 C to target a faster maximum-score method. Lowering temperature from injection 12 should separate its limiting pair, while the steeper gradient may preserve separation of the other close middle pair.

Shorten injection 13’s gradient by two minutes to test the fastest fully resolved method in this region. Monitor both close middle pairs, particularly the pair at R = 1.77 that may lose separation as the gradient steepens.

Test whether lowering the starting organic fraction restores the limiting middle-pair separation despite a slightly steeper gradient. This could retain full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 13; also monitor the other close pair at R = 1.61.

Test a substantially steeper gradient at 60 C to see whether the nearly co-eluting middle pair separates on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover. This explores a faster region while retaining injection 15 as the shortest verified maximum-score method.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity using injection 1’s gradient to test whether the crowded middle cluster separates after a different order shift. This also checks whether a shorter maximum-score method exists outside the extensively tested high-temperature region.

Explore the steep-gradient side of the 60 C selectivity crossover for a substantially faster separation. Lowering the starting organic fraction protects early retention, while this run tests whether the middle cluster can remain resolved under stronger gradient compression.

Test intermediate-temperature selectivity with a steeper gradient to seek a faster fully resolved separation. At 50 C the early pair should be better retained than in injection 11, while the middle cluster may benefit from the combined temperature and slope shift.

Test the unmeasured 35 C selectivity region with a moderately shallow gradient and trimmed starting window. This may separate the middle cluster on the lower-temperature side of its crossover while keeping the last peak earlier than the verified 40 C methods.

Trim injection 15’s unused high-organic segment while preserving its exact gradient slope and temperature. The last peak’s estimated elution fraction is 0.57, so all peaks should elute before the gradient ends and retain the maximum CRF.

Test a slope between injections 13 and 14, targeting the threshold for full resolution with a last peak near 7.6 minutes. This fine adjustment may slightly shorten the best verified separation while preserving the maximum CRF.

Increase the slope slightly from the fastest verified maximum-score method to test whether its small resolution margins permit earlier elution. This directly brackets the speed limit at the most successful starting fraction and temperature.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 22 to bring its R = 1.47 pair above 1.5 while preserving the other close pair’s separation. This targets a near-fastest maximum-score method with a trimmed gradient endpoint above the observed elution window.

Use a different endpoint and duration while preserving the successful 0.075 organic-fraction-per-minute slope. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, reproducing the shortest verified maximum-score separation without changing its critical selectivity.
